questions.q: According to this lesson, when is a migration actually finished?
options: As soon as the data copy process reports success
As soon as the source server is powered off
As soon as SSMS can successfully connect to the new target
When row counts match, query performance is comparable, and application connectivity is confirmed working — not simply when data finishes copying
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates "data finished copying" from "migration actually done," requiring three concrete confirmations.

questions.q: Why does the lesson specify checking application connectivity, not just SSMS connectivity?
options: Because the real application uses its own connection string, authentication, and firewall path, which can fail even when SSMS connects fine
Because SSMS and applications always use identical connection methods
Because SSMS connectivity is impossible to test before cutover
Because applications never need firewall rules configured
questions.explain: SSMS connecting successfully doesn't guarantee the actual application's connection string, auth, or firewall path also works.

questions.q: What does the row-count validation query in this lesson reuse from earlier in Chapter 12?
options: The same system-catalog query skill used for the migration inventory in Lesson 70, now applied to prove the migration worked
A PowerShell cmdlet unrelated to system catalog views
An Azure CLI command with no T-SQL involved
A brand-new scripting language introduced only in this lesson
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects this query back to the Lesson 70 inventory step — same skill, redirected toward validation.

questions.q: Which three common failure patterns does this lesson say to check first when something breaks post-cutover?
options: A missing Elastic Job target group
An expired SSL certificate, a DNS outage, and a full disk
A corrupted backup file, a missing index, and an outdated statistics cache
Connection string/firewall mismatch, a login never recreated as a contained user, and a collation mismatch
questions.explain: These are the specific post-cutover failure patterns this lesson calls out as the places to look first.

questions.q: Why can a login work fine on the source server but fail to authenticate on the migrated target, per this lesson?
options: Because firewall rules always block all logins by default after migration
Because logins only work with Managed Instance, never Azure SQL Database
Because passwords are always reset automatically during any migration
Because SQL logins don't migrate automatically, and the login-to-user mapping must be recreated as a contained user on the target
questions.explain: Missing login-to-contained-user recreation is one of the lesson's named common failure patterns.
